C:title: Forklift Theory Practice (LF)
C:summary: Learn and practise forklift theory for your LF licence assessment — at your own pace, on any device.
C:description: Learn and practise the forklift theory you'll be assessed on for your LF High Risk Work Licence: WHS law and standards, hazards, ground conditions and weather, traffic management, pre-start and operational checks, faults and lock out/tag out, stability, rated capacity, load weight and load centre calculations, attachments, safe operating and stacking, shutdown, refuelling and recharging. Each module ends with a quiz, and a final practice exam helps you check your knowledge. An independent study aid to use alongside your training with an RTO — not nationally recognised training, and it does not give you a licence.
T:high-risk-work-licence: The forklift High Risk Work Licence
L:high-risk-work-licence:1: Operating a forklift is **high risk work** under Australia's Work Health and Safety (WHS) laws. To operate one you must hold a **High Risk Work Licence (HRWL)** for the right class — or be a trainee working under supervision while you train.
L:high-risk-work-licence:2:
| Class | Covers |
|---|---|
| **LF** | Forklift truck (counterbalance, reach trucks and similar) |
| **LO** | Order-picking forklift truck |
L:high-risk-work-licence:5: 2. Pass a knowledge **and** practical assessment with an **accredited assessor**.
L:high-risk-work-licence:6: 3. Apply to your state or territory regulator (e.g. SafeWork NSW, WorkSafe Victoria, WorkSafe Queensland) within the required time.
L:high-risk-work-licence:7: You must be **at least 18**. Licences are recognised nationally and must be renewed (generally every five years).
L:high-risk-work-licence:8: > This online course is theory preparation. It does not on its own give you a licence.
L:whs-duties:1: WHS laws (in Victoria, the OHS Act) place duties on everyone at a workplace.
L:whs-duties:2:
**The business (PCBU / employer) must**, so far as is reasonably practicable:
- provide safe plant — a forklift that is maintained and fit for use
- provide information, training, instruction and supervision
- set up safe systems of work, such as a **traffic management plan**
L:whs-duties:3:
**As an operator you must:**
- take reasonable care for your own health and safety
- take reasonable care that what you do (or don't do) doesn't harm others
- follow reasonable instructions, policies and **workplace procedures**
- **report hazards, incidents and defects**
L:whs-duties:5: Your instructions may come as a **verbal** instruction from a supervisor, a **written** job sheet, safe work procedure or SWMS, or an **electronic** work order on a scanner or tablet. Whatever form they take: read or listen carefully, ask questions if anything is unclear, and follow them.
T:standards-codes-records: Standards, codes of practice and records
L:standards-codes-records:1:
| Source | What it is |
|---|---|
| **WHS Act and Regulations** | The law. Must be followed. |
| **Codes of practice** | Practical guidance on meeting the law — e.g. Safe Work Australia's *Managing the risks of plant in the workplace*. Courts can use them as evidence of what is reasonably practicable. |
| **Australian Standards** | Technical requirements — e.g. the **AS 2359** series for powered industrial trucks (forklifts). |
| **Guidelines** | Further guidance — e.g. Safe Work Australia's *General guide for workplace traffic management*. |
| **Manufacturer's manual** | How *this* forklift must be operated, checked and maintained. |
| **Workplace procedures** | How *your site* does things — traffic plan, SWMS, emergency procedures. |
L:standards-codes-records:3: Good records prove checks were done and problems were followed up:
L:standards-codes-records:7: - **Maintenance and service records** for the forklift
L:standards-codes-records:8: - **Trainee logbook** — if you're training, record your supervised operating hours
L:standards-codes-records:9: Records must be **accurate, legible, dated and signed**, and kept where your workplace procedures say.
L:planning-and-communication:1: - **The load** — weight, size, shape, centre of gravity; is it stable and secure?
L:planning-and-communication:2: - **The forklift** — is the load within its **rated capacity**? Is the right attachment fitted?
L:planning-and-communication:3: - **The route** — surfaces, slopes, doorways, overhead clearances, blind corners.
L:planning-and-communication:4: - **The destination** — racking capacity, where the load will be placed.
L:planning-and-communication:5: - **People** — who else is working nearby, and how will you communicate?
L:planning-and-communication:7:
| Method | Use it for |
|---|---|
| **Warning devices** — horn, flashing beacon, reversing alarm, lights | Alerting people to the forklift |
| **Hand signals** | Directions from a spotter or observer. Agree the signals **before** starting. |
| **Two-way radio** | Coordinating over distance. Use clear, short messages and confirm you've understood. |
| **Signage and traffic warning systems** | Speed limits, pedestrian crossings, no-go zones, warning lights at doorways |
| **Written instructions** | Job sheets, work orders, SWMS, consignment paperwork |
| **Verbal instructions and questioning** | Ask questions to check you understand — e.g. "So you want these three pallets in bay 4, top level?" |
L:planning-and-communication:8: Always make **eye contact with pedestrians** before moving near them.
L:hazards-and-controls:1: - **Pedestrians**, other plant and vehicles — collision risk
L:hazards-and-controls:2: - **Overhead hazards** — powerlines (see the next lesson), low beams, doorways, sprinklers, lights, fixed structures
L:hazards-and-controls:4: - **Dangerous goods** — check labels/placards and the Safety Data Sheet (SDS); know the spill procedure
L:hazards-and-controls:5: - **Restricted or poorly ventilated areas** — LPG, petrol and diesel forklifts give off **carbon monoxide** in exhaust
L:hazards-and-controls:8: ## Hazard or risk — what's the difference?
L:hazards-and-controls:9: - A **hazard** is anything that **could cause harm** — injury, illness or damage. It's the *thing* or *situation*: a pedestrian near your work area, an oil spill, a powerline, a pothole, a damaged pallet.
L:hazards-and-controls:10: - A **risk** is the **chance that the hazard will actually hurt someone, and how bad it would be**. It's about *likelihood* and *consequence*.
L:hazards-and-controls:11:
| Hazard (what could cause harm) | Risk (how likely, and how bad) |
|---|---|
| Pedestrians walking through the loading area | Being struck by the forklift — likely in a busy area, and could be fatal |
| Oil spill on the floor | The forklift skids or someone slips — likely if it's on your route |
| Overhead powerline near the yard | Electrocution if the mast gets close — less likely if you plan, but the consequence is death |
| Damaged pallet | The load collapses or falls — injury or damaged stock |
L:hazards-and-controls:12: > **Spot the hazard → assess the risk → control it.** The hazard is the thing; the risk is how likely and how serious the harm is.
L:hazards-and-controls:14: Ask two questions about each hazard:
L:hazards-and-controls:15: 1. **Likelihood** — how likely is it to cause harm? (*Rare, possible, likely*)
L:hazards-and-controls:16: 2. **Consequence** — if it does, how bad would it be? (*Minor first aid, serious injury, death*)
L:hazards-and-controls:17: A hazard that is **likely** to happen **and** could cause **serious injury or death** is a **high risk** — fix it before you start work. Low risks still need controlling.
L:hazards-and-controls:19: 1. **Identify** the hazards — walk the route and look around before you start.
L:hazards-and-controls:21: 3. **Control** it using the hierarchy of control.
L:hazards-and-controls:22: 4. **Review** — are the controls working? Has anything changed?
L:hazards-and-controls:24: Use the most effective control you can, then work down:
L:hazards-and-controls:27: 3. **Isolate** people from it (barriers, separate walkways, exclusion zones)
L:hazards-and-controls:31: If a control is missing or not working, **report it**.
T:powerlines: Powerlines: keep clear, and the 5-step contact protocol
L:powerlines:1: Overhead powerlines are one of the deadliest hazards for forklift operators. Electricity can **jump (arc)** across a gap — you don't have to touch the line to be electrocuted. Treat **every line as live**.
L:powerlines:2: Before you start work outdoors or near doorways and awnings:
L:powerlines:3: - **Look up** — find every overhead line before you move or raise the mast.
L:powerlines:4: - **Keep the minimum approach distance** for your state and the line's voltage. For example, SafeWork NSW sets **3 m** for lines up to 132,000 volts, **6 m** up to 330,000 volts and **8 m** above that. Your site may set a bigger distance.
L:powerlines:5: - Remember lines **sag** in heat and **swing** in wind — and a raised mast or load is higher than you think.
L:powerlines:6: - **Lower the mast and tynes** before you travel near lines.
L:powerlines:7: - Use a **spotter** when working near lines, and ask for the power to be **switched off or the lines covered** if you have to work close to them.
